reasons: Lake record is verified for Michigan v. Clifford with U.S. Supreme Court, date decided 1984-01-11, and year 1984.
Lake official citation is 464 U.S. 287; parallel citations are 104 S. Ct. 641, 78 L. Ed. 2d 477, and 52 U.S.L.W. 4056; vendor-neutral citation is 1984 U.S. LEXIS 14.
Opinion text states that if reasonable privacy interests remain in fire-damaged property, the warrant requirement applies absent consent or exigent circumstances.

Opinion text states that postfire investigations begun after the fire is out and officials have left generally require a warrant or a new exigency, and that administrative versus criminal warrant type turns on the search object.
Opinion text applies those rules to the Clifford home and holds the warrantless basement and upstairs searches unconstitutional except for the driveway fuel can.
residual_risks: The proposition is a compressed synthesis; the most precise home-specific formulation includes that fire and police units had left and the homeowners had acted to secure the residence.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Specify that the stronger home-specific holding applies where officials have left the scene and the homeowner has made a reasonable effort to secure the fire-damaged home.

reasons: The opinion recognizes a burning building as an exigency justifying warrantless entry to fight the blaze, but limits later postfire entries once reasonable privacy interests remain and no new exigency is identified.
That makes the case a limiting authority for emergency or exigency-based warrantless entry in the fire context.
residual_risks: The disclosed files do not define the corpus page title Emergency Aid; if that page is limited to aid-to-persons doctrine rather than emergency/exigency entries generally, the home placement would need taxonomy review.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: If the taxonomy distinguishes fire exigency from aid-to-persons emergency aid, place this primarily under an exigent-circumstances/fire-emergency home and keep Emergency Aid only as related.

reasons: The opinion expressly discusses administrative searches and says administrative searches generally require warrants.
The opinion states that an administrative warrant suffices when the primary object is to determine the cause and origin of a recent fire, while evidence-gathering requires a criminal warrant.

Content treatment fields match the lake treatment judgment fields: good_law, as_of_content 1984-01-11, as_of_treatment 2026-06-30, migration-seed basis, no point variation, and the same plurality scope note.
Treatment merits are outside Lens A; no independent treatment/currency finding is raised.
residual_risks: Lake treatment derivation includes audit markers and progeny data that are for Lens B, not this support/quote-fidelity review.
